title: Scientists develop new method for deciphering ancient scrolls
gist: A team led by retired inventor Douglas Seiler built and deliberately carbonized modern papyrus scrolls inked with varying lead concentrations to validate a cheap screening method — even a handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner — for identifying which Herculaneum scrolls contain lead-based ink and are therefore easiest to read. Published in PLoS ONE, the work could sharply accelerate the Vesuvius Challenge, which has already paid a $700,000 grand prize and fully read PHerc. 1667.

insights.claim: Researchers created contemporary model papyrus scrolls and charred them to mimic the originals in order to validate a screening method for determining which ancient scrolls were written in lead-based ink, publishing the process in PLoS ONE.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Manufacturing destroyable proxies of irreplaceable artifacts is a transferable validation pattern for any field working with unique, fragile samples.
insights.locator: A team of researchers created their own contemporary model papyrus scrolls

insights.claim: The team purchased modern Egyptian papyrus, still prepared much as it was two millennia ago, and traditional lampblack ink from Japan, then added different amounts of lead nitrate to produce samples with controlled lead concentrations.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The experimental inputs are cheap and commercially available, meaning other groups can replicate the calibration set immediately.
insights.locator: The authors purchased modern Egyptian papyrus

insights.claim: A team of high school students inscribed the model papyri with a reed stylus using quotes from the Bible, Star Wars and the 1960s TV show The Outer Limits, and the scrolls were CT-scanned to verify their lead concentrations before carbonization.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Ground-truth text of known content is what makes the validation rigorous — the researchers knew exactly what the scans should reveal.
insights.locator: A team of high school students inscribed the papyri

insights.claim: After carbonizing the model scrolls in a high-temperature furnace, physicist Jake LaManna produced 3D X-ray scans at NIST's Center for Neutron Research in Maryland, with Seiler reporting that 'the letters lit up like a Christmas tree.'
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A dramatic contrast improvement over carbon ink is the entire commercial and scientific case for the lead-screening approach.
insights.quote: The letters lit up like a Christmas tree
insights.locator: said Seiler, adding, “It’s amazing what you can get electrons to do.”

insights.claim: Co-author Michael Cyrus Daugherty of NIST digitally unwrapped the model scrolls by adapting software he had originally written to unroll CT scans of the 'jelly rolls' inside lithium-ion batteries.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A striking cross-domain transfer: battery-inspection tooling directly repurposed for classical archaeology.
insights.locator: adapted a software program he’d written to unroll CT scans

themes.theme: Why carbon ink is the bottleneck

insights.claim: Many inks used by Egyptian scribes contained large traces of metals including lead, making them ideal for X-ray imaging, whereas the older Herculaneum scrolls used carbon-based ink of charcoal and water that produces almost no difference in X-ray absorption between inked and blank papyrus.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The physical contrast problem, not computing power, is the root constraint on reading these texts.
insights.locator: Many of the inks used by Egyptian scribes contained large traces of metals

insights.claim: In 2016 scientists identified letters in two fragments of a scroll that contained lead, suggesting some Herculaneum scrolls might be written in lead-based ink — the observation that prompted Seiler's screening project.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A decade-old incidental finding became the seed of a systematic triage strategy.
insights.locator: In 2016, scientists identified letters in two fragments of a scroll that contained lead

insights.claim: Seiler argues teams should prioritize searching for lead because 'with lead in the ink, you would get a huge friggin' signature,' whereas current difficulties stem from 'the low contrast of carbon ink on carbon paper.'
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Reordering which scrolls get scanned first could deliver readable texts far faster than improving the algorithms.
insights.quote: They’re having problems reading a lot of them because of the low contrast of carbon ink on carbon paper

insights.claim: Even a handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner is sufficient to determine which scrolls are the most promising candidates for further analysis, making the triage step cheap and portable.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Low-cost, non-destructive screening could be deployed at libraries holding the scrolls without shipping them to synchrotrons.
insights.locator: Even a handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner is sufficient

insights.claim: Seiler offered '10-to-1 odds' that scrolls containing lead will be readable much more easily, and said he does not care whether his own team or another executes the idea.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: An explicit odds statement is a rare, falsifiable commitment from a researcher about a method's payoff.
insights.quote: I’ll give you 10-to-1 odds. We’d like it to be our team, but if some other team is going to take this idea—which is OK—we don’t care.

insights.claim: The Vesuvius Challenge combines 'digital unwrapping' with crowdsourced machine learning to decipher the Herculaneum papyri, which are too fragile to physically unroll after 2,000 years of carbonization.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A crowdsourced prize structure applied to a scientific imaging problem is an organizational model worth noting in its own right.
insights.locator: The Vesuvius Challenge is an ongoing project

insights.claim: Brent Searles' lab at the University of Kentucky pioneered virtual unrolling, using micro-computed tomography — a noninvasive technique often used for cancer imaging — plus segmentation, texturing and flattening, with software called Volume Cartography.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Medical imaging hardware is the enabling substrate for the entire field — another cross-domain dependency.
insights.locator: The team’s approach combined digital scanning with micro-computed tomography

insights.claim: Searles used the method in 2016 to virtually open the En Gedi scroll — a lump of charcoal recovered from an ancient synagogue destroyed by fire around 600 CE — revealing the first verses of the book of Leviticus.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Proof the technique recovers real text from apparently destroyed artifacts, establishing credibility for the harder Herculaneum case.
insights.locator: which he used in 2016 to “open” a scroll found on the western shore of the Dead Sea

insights.claim: Because carbon ink produces no X-ray fluorescence contrast, Searles instead captured minute textural differences in the papyrus and trained an artificial neural network to detect them.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Machine learning is compensating for a physics limitation — which is why removing the physics limitation via lead screening is so valuable.
insights.locator: Searles was still able to capture minute textural differences

themes.theme: Progress and provenance of the scrolls

insights.claim: The Vesuvius Challenge made its first award for deciphering initial letters in 2023, awarded a $700,000 grand prize the following year for the first readable text, produced the first X-ray image of the inside of PHerc. 172 at Oxford's Bodleian Libraries last year, and earlier this year fully read PHerc. 1667, a philosophical treatise on ethics and human moral progress.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: A clear acceleration curve: from first letters to a fully read treatise in roughly three years.
insights.locator: which made its first award for deciphering the first letters in 2023

insights.claim: More than 600 rolled-up Herculaneum scrolls survive, excavated in the 1700s from a single room in a palatial residence believed to have belonged to a man named Piso and thought to hold the personal working library of the Epicurean philosopher Philodemus.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The scale — hundreds of unread volumes from one philosophical library — is what makes an efficient triage method consequential.
insights.locator: the more than 600 rolled-up scrolls were so fragile

insights.claim: The scrolls were carbonized when Herculaneum, a wealthy enclave near Pompeii, was destroyed by pyroclastic pulses and flows during the 79 AD eruption of Mount Vesuvius.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The same event that destroyed the library is what preserved it — the carbonization is both the damage and the reason the texts survived.
insights.locator: the catastrophic 79 AD eruption of Mount Vesuvius

insights.claim: Douglas Seiler, a retired inventor, was working with Berkeley SETI on a telescope called Panoseti when he learned of the Herculaneum scrolls and the poor signal-to-noise ratios plaguing digital unwrapping efforts.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: Signal-processing expertise from astronomy transferring into archaeology is the kind of adjacency that produces step-change methods.
insights.locator: Douglas Seiler, a retired inventor, was working with Berkeley SETI

insights.claim: Seiler assembled an interdisciplinary team including two retired Berkeley chemists and a Berkeley graduate student in archaeology with expertise in ancient Egyptian inks, and described the combination of 'inorganic chemistry, papyrus, X-ray tomography, AI' as being as unique as the research itself.
insights.speaker: Jennifer Ouellette
insights.so_what: The result depended on assembling retired specialists across four fields — an argument for unconventional team composition over institutional pipelines.
insights.quote: inorganic chemistry, papyrus, X-ray tomography, AI—it’s really quite an eclectic group of scientists and methodology
insights.locator: “Honestly, getting here is, for me, just as unique as our research,” Seiler said
